messages.author: 238a8b6ad34ddf1f
messages.subject: Seasonality as a covariate
parts:
Hi all, 

I have data on bobcat and coyote conflict from 2019 to 2023, I'm trying to figure out how to add seasonality (Winter, Spring, Summer, Fall) as a site covariate. Has anyone done this before?

I am thinking of adding a column for seasonality, and assigning numbers to each sighting based on the incident date. 

Any advice? TIA!
Carly

 What kind of model are you looking at? I assume an occupancy model. And is this a 2-species Rota-type model or what, exactly?  And should season affect occupancy or detection?
 regards

messages.author: 4a15de51da4445ae
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Seasonality as a covariate
parts:
hi Carly,
 I think you want season to be an observation covariate, assuming your sample occasions are daily, weekly or monthly periods and you have a few of them.  So you need a matrix of values:  nsites x nocassions , and each value of this matrix should be the day of the sample occasion or the mid-point of the interval or whatever.  And then you can model p as a linear or quadratic function of "day of year".    It's possible you want to have a season-specific p in which case you can create a factor variable ("winter", "spring" "summer" "fall") and if you use that variable in the model for p then you'll get 4 different values of p.
 
 Maybe there's more structure to your data that would suggest otherwise, but this is where I would start.

regards
andy

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Seasonality as a covariate
parts:
Hi Carly,

As an addition to Andy's inputs: if you coerce the data into an occupancy structure, I previously used season as a categorical site covariate (winter/summer) by dividing each site into seasons and giving detection/non-detection data according to that.

For example if you have Site1 and a detection in occasion(s) that fall under summer category and no detection for occasion(s) that fall under winter category:
- divide Site1 as Site1W and Site1S
- in the nsites x noccasions matrix Site1W will have 0 and Site1S will have 1. 
(of course your nsites will double in amount).

I did this in a Bayesian model, did not try with unmarked but it should work the same.
I hope I could make myself clear and it helps.

Best,
Dilsad
On Mon, Apr 8, 2024 at 1:05 AM Jeffrey Royle <jar...@gmail.com> wrote:

hi Carly, 
 ok so the data could be coerced into an occupancy data structure by using months or some other smaller interval as a "replicate" I think (or 3 month period or whatever).   I think what I said previously still holds then.  
regards
andy


On Sun, Apr 7, 2024 at 6:50 PM Carly Thompson <car...@umich.edu> wrote:
Hi Andy, 

Thank you, I think it might be helpful if I described my data structure. I have incidents for the state of CA and am looking at them at the tract level - 8,057 census tracts from 2019 to 2023, and each year is my site. So I have counts per census tract and covariates for state. I am trying to add seasonality for detection and trying to figure out how to structure it. 



My raw data is the incident date with lat/long which I added to arcGIS to calculate the census tract. 

Carly Thompson (she/her/hers)
Masters Candidate, Dual Focus
Ecosystem Science & Management
Geospatial Data Science
LinkedIn | CoCoLab



On Sun, Apr 7, 2024 at 6:22 PM Jeffrey Royle <jar...@gmail.com> wrote:
hi Carly,
 I think you want season to be an observation covariate, assuming your sample occasions are daily, weekly or monthly periods and you have a few of them.  So you need a matrix of values:  nsites x nocassions , and each value of this matrix should be the day of the sample occasion or the mid-point of the interval or whatever.  And then you can model p as a linear or quadratic function of "day of year".    It's possible you want to have a season-specific p in which case you can create a factor variable ("winter", "spring" "summer" "fall") and if you use that variable in the model for p then you'll get 4 different values of p.
 
 Maybe there's more structure to your data that would suggest otherwise, but this is where I would start.

regards
andy
